items.title: Bob Havens interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997
items.q: So I decided to go with his orchestra in 1960.

ctx.x: Okay. Well tell me about Lawrence Welk.

Lawrence Welk, okay. Well I got started, I went and played in a Dixieland band and in Al Hirt’s band, and of course Mr. Welk got his start back in the thirties and worked his way up as a big orchestra leader, and he developed a style known as the “champagne style” which is kind of a bubbly sound, like Shep Fields. They were both going in the same direction. Well Mr. Welk came through town and stopped in at this Dance Pier 600 where I was working with Al Hirt, and he listened to the band all evening. And he liked…
Excuse me, was this pre-TV? Was he traveling the country like other bands?

items.title: Bob Havens interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997
items.q: I have been introduced to the Lawrence Welk stage show, I’m now working in the band at the theatre

ctx.x: And this was basically an every-day, like a full time job for you, right?

Well now that I have been introduced to the Lawrence Welk stage show, I’m now working in the band at the theatre, I’ve discovered that it’s much, much harder to do a stage production than it is television. A television show — I did it for twenty-two years — and there was a different program every week. We would rehearse two days. One day was sound rehearsal and the other day was sound and video. Well it involved about nineteen hours totally for each weekly show. Well I’m doing this theatre thing now, and I’m…
The Lennon Daughters. Gee, it must be like — to keep your concentration is probably —
